claims.text: Adding a minor amount of boron to a conventional alloy melt should enhance its glass-forming ability.
Boron is an element capable of having a highly negative heat of mixing with the primary metallic elements in the alloy.
The baseline alloy normally requires rapid quenching to avoid crystallization.
A boron addition of roughly 1–5 at% is a suitable minor-alloying intervention.
The boron intervention can improve glass formation under melting and casting conditions with relatively slow cooling rates.
Adding boron promotes formation of a deep-eutectic-type melt composition.
The deep-eutectic-type composition depresses the liquidus temperature.
A highly negative heat of mixing between boron and the primary metallic elements lowers the liquidus temperature.
Boron addition kinetically suppresses crystal nucleation.
Lowering the liquidus temperature and suppressing nucleation increase the stability of the liquid against crystallization.
The increased stability of the liquid creates a broader processing window.
The boron-containing alloy will retain an amorphous structure at slower cooling rates than the corresponding boron-free alloy.
The corresponding boron-free alloy crystallizes unless it is quenched extremely rapidly.
The boron concentration must remain low to avoid formation of secondary phases.
Excessive boron may negatively affect desired mechanical properties.
Other elements with highly negative heats of mixing might produce similar improvements in glass-forming ability.
